Evidence repository

The Development Impact of Digital Transformation and AI

A searchable repository of 527 studies on what digital technology actually does to growth, jobs, firms, welfare, inclusion, the public sector and the environment — organized by digital topic and outcome, by whether a study evaluates a policy reform, an investment or the adoption of a technology, and by how credibly it identifies a causal effect. Where the underlying paper reports them, each entry carries the method, the data and the estimated magnitude.

261 of 527 entries use an experimental or quasi-experimental design Last updated 15 October 2026

Evidence summary

What the repository says, topic by topic: the headline findings with their reported magnitudes, the mechanisms behind them, and where the evidence runs thin. Every figure is taken from a study in the repository — follow the citation to the paper. Counts update with the data; the narrative reflects the evidence as of 15 October 2026.

Broadband & internet infrastructure121 studies · 67 causalSolid experimental and quasi-experimental evidence shows connectivity raises jobs and welfare: randomized tower placement raised rural Philippine household income 17% Blumenstock et al. (2024); fast internet raised African employment probability 6.9-13.2 percentage points Hjort and Poulsen (2019). Reform evidence is thinner, mostly on prices and coverage in high-income markets.

What the evidence shows

  • Randomized placement of mobile towers in the rural Philippines raised annual household income 17%, benefiting self-employed and migrant workers most Blumenstock et al. (2024). Quasi-experimental estimates find fast internet raised employment probability 6.9-13.2 percentage points in Africa, especially in higher-skill occupations Hjort and Poulsen (2019), and GSM-era mobile coverage raised the local employment rate in rural South Africa about 15 percentage points, mostly among women Klonner and Nolen (2010).
  • Mobile broadband coverage raised Nigerian household consumption by more than 10%, driven mainly by rising employment, especially among women, in a difference-in-differences study coauthored by GSMA staff Bahia et al. (2024); in Senegal, 3G coverage was associated with 14% higher consumption and 10% less extreme poverty, more for urban and male-headed households Masaki et al. (2020). In a 116-country difference-in-differences study, 3G arrival also reduced confidence in national government Guriev et al. (2021).
  • Quasi-experimental studies find submarine-cable arrival expanded African bank credit supply 22% D'Andrea and Limodio (2024) and ultra-fast broadband raised Italian firms' total factor productivity 2.9% Cambini et al. (2023). OECD instrumental-variable estimates link a 10-percentage-point rise in broadband penetration to 0.9-1.5 percentage points faster annual GDP per capita growth Czernich et al. (2009); below USD 12,000 GDP per capita, model-based associations are positive for mobile broadband and zero for fixed broadband ITU (2020).
  • A quasi-experimental preprint finds developing-country tower-sharing deals cut data prices $1.00 per GB from a $3.41 baseline and HHI 5.3% Houngbonon et al. (2025). The internet-access gain for women-headed households (3.2 points in the baseline) persists, but the rural gain is concentrated in the deal year and fades after two years; sale-and-leaseback deals outperform acquisitions on voice tariffs, with no meaningful difference for data prices Houngbonon et al. (2025).
  • A GSMA-coauthored difference-in-differences study of 140 European operators links sharing to 5.6 percentage points higher 4G coverage and 100 points lower HHI, though HHI rises when the largest operators (40%+ share) share Koutroumpis et al. (2023). A white paper commissioned by tower company SBA Communications links high independent tower ownership in Africa to 8.09 percentage points higher 4G coverage, but its evidence is correlational and model-based Katz et al. (2024).
  • Instrumental-variable estimates by GSMA staff link a 1% rise in spectrum cost to 0.53 percentage points lower 4G coverage in developing countries Bahia and Castells (2022). Structural simulations find earlier licensing of Rwanda's second operator would have cut prices 30-50% Björkegren (2022). In a developing-country panel, reforms combining privatization and competition with an independent regulator were associated with 8% more mainlines than partial or no reform Fink et al. (2003).
  • Instrumental-variable estimates find OECD state aid raised fiber connections 22 percentage points of households short term and 39.3 long term Briglauer and Grajek (2024). French subsidies sped early fiber coverage, but structural estimates find that in 36% of cases they went where private entry would have occurred within three years Bourreau et al. (2026). Panel estimates find E-Rate subsidies raised connected classrooms in California about 68% without significant test-score gains Goolsbee and Guryan (2006).

Mechanisms

  • Lower search costs: in natural experiments, mobile coverage cut Nigerien grain price dispersion 10-16% Aker (2010), and the share of Kerala fishermen selling outside their home market rose from zero to about 35% as price dispersion and waste collapsed Jensen (2007).
  • Labor reallocation: quasi-experimental estimates show 3G moved men into small enterprises and service wage jobs and women into vacated unpaid farm work and small non-farm businesses, an informal, gig-like pattern Chiplunkar and Goldberg (2022); Rwandan employment shifted toward skill-intensive services Caldarola et al. (2023).
  • Competition and investment trade off: panel estimates show concentration raises prices and per-operator investment, with inconclusive effects on total investment Genakos et al. (2018); mandated wholesale access reduced fixed-line investment Grajek and Röller (2012); tower-sharing deals cut concentration, pointing to competition as their channel Houngbonon et al. (2025).
  • Complements: in quasi-experimental studies, electricity and roads amplified internet-driven FDI in Africa Mensah and Traore (2024), and satellite-delivered lessons by top teachers added 0.75 years of schooling in rural China Bianchi et al. (2022); subsidized classroom connections did not significantly raise California test scores Goolsbee and Guryan (2006).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Investment and public programs dominate the causal evidence on jobs, growth and learning. Policy-reform studies are a sizable minority but mostly measure prices, coverage and operator investment, rarely jobs or growth, never environmental outcomes. Adoption-and-use studies are the smallest group.
  • No causal study evaluates a sharing mandate: developing-country evidence covers voluntary tower deals Houngbonon et al. (2025), and mandate simulations rest on correlational, model-based work commissioned by a tower company Katz et al. (2024). Developing-country universal service funds and operator taxes have only descriptive assessments, for example Jain and Raghuram (2009) and Rota-Graziosi and Sawadogo (2022).
  • Causal evidence on mergers, access regulation and demand-side subsidies is OECD-only, for example Genakos et al. (2018), Grajek and Röller (2012) and Galperin and Bar (2024). Environmental effects are thin and split by income: mobile broadband cut per-capita CO2 only in high-income countries Edquist and Bergmark (2024), while ICT use raised emissions in Sub-Saharan Africa Avom et al. (2020).
  • Impact studies rarely report costs. A model-based costing puts universal connectivity by 2030 at $2.6 to $2.8 trillion, with the policy and regulatory gap about $0.6 billion International Telecommunication Union (2025); the three-year break-even estimated for OECD state aid relies on external output estimates Briglauer and Grajek (2024).

Digital devices34 studies · 17 causalRandomized evidence is strong but mixed: smartphones given to Tanzanian women raised household consumption per capita 20% Roessler et al. (2021), yet laptops for rural Peruvian students produced no detectable learning gains even 10 years later Cueto et al. (2025). Women's ownership often lapses; affordability-policy evidence is thin.

What the evidence shows

  • A randomized trial found smartphones given to women in low-income Tanzanian households raised consumption per capita 20% over 13 months, yet only 34% still had the phone at endline Roessler et al. (2021). Quasi-experimental estimates show an Indian program giving women free smartphones plus new towers reversed the gender gap in ownership, but gains faded within about five years as men appropriated phones Barboni et al. (2024).
  • Randomized laptop programs raised use and some cognitive skills but not test scores: One Laptop per Child in rural Peru raised computers per student from 0.12 to 1.18 without math or language gains after 15 months Cristia et al. (2017) or effects on performance and attainment 10 years later Cueto et al. (2025); take-home laptops in Lima showed the same pattern Beuermann et al. (2015).
  • Programs that use phones show gains: in a randomized trial in Niger, adding mobile-phone use to adult literacy classes raised writing and math scores 0.19-0.26 standard deviations, mostly among women Aker et al. (2012); a review of randomized trials finds digital agricultural advice raised yields about 4% and adoption odds about 22%, though farmers' willingness to pay is low Fabregas et al. (2019).
  • Phone-based mobile money shows consistent gains: quasi-experimental estimates find M-Pesa access lifted about 194,000 Kenyan households, roughly 2%, out of extreme poverty, especially female-headed ones Suri and Jack (2016), and randomized trials find mobile-money rather than cash delivery of loans and transfers raised women's business profits about 15% Riley (2024) and child dietary diversity 9%-16% Aker et al. (2016).
  • Synthetic-control estimates find Colombia's VAT exemption on low-cost handsets raised smartphone penetration 7.6 percentage points Sachidananda et al. (2026). A structural model estimates that India's GST rise on phones from 12% to 18% cut smartphone sales 5.7%, and a targeted $10 subsidy for low-income buyers matches tax cuts' adoption gains far more cheaply Shreeti (2023). Mandatory SIM registration is associated with slower subscription growth in Sub-Saharan Africa Jentzsch (2012).
  • Access and affordability are unequal: industry-association surveys find women in low- and middle-income countries 14% less likely than men to use mobile internet, with about 885 million unconnected and no narrowing in 2024 GSMA (2025); structural estimates find India's bottom 60% about 4 times more price-sensitive than the top 40% Shreeti (2023).
  • A randomized four-week Facebook deactivation raised subjective well-being but reduced news knowledge Allcott et al. (2020), and difference-in-differences estimates find Facebook's staggered arrival at US colleges raised severe depression and anxiety among students Braghieri et al. (2022). Monitoring data show global e-waste reached 62 million metric tons in 2022, only 22.3% formally recycled International Telecommunication Union and UNITAR (2024), and a systematic review links exposure to adverse child health Parvez et al. (2021).

Mechanisms

  • Household control: randomized trials trace smartphone gains to women's control and use of the device Roessler et al. (2021) and show mobile money helps women shield resources from household claims Riley (2024); men's appropriation of shared phones eroded women's gains Barboni et al. (2024).
  • Network externalities: structural estimates attribute 73-76% of the extra operator revenue from a Rwandan rural handset subsidy to non-recipients Bjorkegren and Karaca (2020), and subsidizing well-connected hub users generates larger diffusion spillovers than random or income-targeted subsidies Bjorkegren (2019).
  • Skills and content: randomized digital-literacy training made women's smartphone use and mental-health gains last Barboni et al. (2024); in randomized trials, phone use built into a literacy curriculum raised test scores Aker et al. (2012), but providing laptops did not Cristia et al. (2017).
  • Lower transaction costs: difference-in-differences estimates show mobile money let users absorb income shocks that cut nonusers' consumption 7%, through more remittances from a wider set of senders Jack and Suri (2014).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Most causal evidence concerns investment and public programs, such as device handouts, laptops and mobile-money rollout, followed by adoption and use; policy reform has only a few causal studies, on handset taxes, a US subsidy and SIM registration. No causal study covers firms.
  • No causal study evaluates device financing; proposals such as removing taxes on sub-$100 handsets rest on industry modeling GSMA Intelligence (2024), and the case that Colombia's VAT exemption could offset its revenue losses rests on a preliminary cost-benefit analysis Sachidananda et al. (2026).
  • Long-run evidence is scarce: most device trials follow participants for about a year or less, and longer follow-ups find null learning effects after 10 years Cueto et al. (2025) and fading ownership gains for women Barboni et al. (2024).
  • Evidence on people with disabilities and refugees is descriptive, for example Pacheco and Burgess (2024) and the partly industry-authored UNHCR, ITU, and GSMA (2024); e-waste health harms rest on associational studies Parvez et al. (2021), and no study evaluates recycling or take-back policy.

Internet exchange points8 studies · 1 causalEvidence is thin and mostly descriptive: a before-and-after case study credits Kenya's exchange with cutting domestic latency from 200-600ms to 2-10ms Internet Society (2020), and a cross-country panel links peering savings to lower broadband prices Tagat and Phokeer (2026). No study measures effects on growth or jobs.

What the evidence shows

  • A cross-country panel for 2019-2024 finds peering substantially cheaper than IP transit; larger savings are associated with lower consumer broadband prices, wider mobile coverage and higher telecom revenues, most clearly in moderately regulated and low- and lower-middle-income economies Tagat and Phokeer (2026). These associations do not isolate the effect of building or expanding an exchange.
  • A before-and-after case study reports that Kenya's exchange cut domestic latency from 200-600ms to 2-10ms and saved local ISPs nearly USD 1.5 million a year in international connectivity costs in 2012, about USD 6 million by 2020; Nigeria's saved operators close to USD 1 million a year, and the locally exchanged traffic share rose from about 30% to 70% Internet Society (2020).
  • A small measurement study in Italy found about 70% of probes routed via IXPs had average round-trip times of 30ms or less versus 20% of others, and about 80% of non-IXP paths crossed a foreign network even for domestic traffic, with the largest gains for smaller networks di Lallo (2015).
  • A continental diagnostic with a 2018 baseline found 42% of African countries had no IXP and only about 44 IXPs served 32 countries, so most domestic traffic was routed through international hubs at international transit prices Broadband Commission Working Group on Broadband (2019).
  • A difference-in-differences study finds the EU's GDPR had precisely zero short-run effect on the number and type of interconnection agreements between EEA and non-EEA networks and only economically small effects on network entry and customer counts, despite the law's substantial compliance costs for application firms Zhuo et al. (2021).

Mechanisms

  • Traffic localization: measurements show peering at exchanges keeps domestic traffic off foreign networks, reducing latency, hop count, packet loss and jitter di Lallo (2015); case-study data show locally exchanged traffic grew in Kenya and Nigeria between 2012 and 2020 Internet Society (2020).
  • Transit-cost savings: in a cross-country panel, peering is substantially cheaper than IP transit and larger savings go with lower broadband prices, consistent with pass-through Tagat and Phokeer (2026); Kenyan ISPs' annual savings grew as local traffic exchange expanded Internet Society (2020).
  • Content localization: a measurement study shows Netflix embeds caching servers within ISPs and at IXPs rather than relying on centralized hosting or paid transit, making exchanges a cornerstone of its content delivery Böttger et al. (2018).
  • Peering formation: at Milan's exchange, ISPs with shorter travel times between headquarters, higher bandwidth and fewer alternative European IXP connections were more likely to peer, in descriptive probit estimates Giovannetti et al. (2003).

Where the evidence is thin

  • The only quasi-experimental study is a GDPR evaluation Zhuo et al. (2021), a policy reform; the cross-country peering-cost panel is correlational Tagat and Phokeer (2026), and no causal study concerns adoption and use. No causal study covers growth, firms, jobs, human capital or environment.
  • No study evaluates IXP regulation, public or donor funding, or governance models, and none reports what an exchange costs to build or run; a model-based costing bundles IXPs with last-mile networks, backbone and data centers International Telecommunication Union (2025).
  • Country-specific African evidence is a before-and-after case study of Kenya and Nigeria Internet Society (2020) and a continental diagnostic Broadband Commission Working Group on Broadband (2019); network measurements come mainly from Italy di Lallo (2015). No study tracks whether a new exchange attracts data centers or local digital firms over time.

Data centers52 studies · 8 causalUS-only quasi-experimental evidence is mixed: a county's first large data center raises data-processing employment 56% over a decade, roughly 100-200 jobs Bahar and Wright (2026), but a site-level study finds no salary or firm-entry spillovers Bahar and Wright (2026). Electricity-price estimates conflict; environmental costs rest on projections.

What the evidence shows

  • Job estimates range from null to moderate. A staggered difference-in-differences finds longer-run gains of 3.5% in employment and 5.0% in total wages, negligible outside metro counties Yue and Zeng (2026); a site-level design rules out advertised-salary gains above 5.5%, with rents up 2-5% Bahar and Wright (2026). A shift-share IV finds house prices up 17.7% per log point of data-center revenue Alvarez et al. (2026), but Bahar and Wright (2026) rejects that type of instrument.
  • Quasi-experimental price estimates conflict, partly by design, market and period: residential rates fall about 3.5% per doubling of state data-center capacity Watten et al. (2026); local retail prices show no detectable rise Garcia-Appendini et al. (2025), Bahar and Wright (2026) or rise roughly 5% Yue and Zeng (2026); and in PJM zones after AI model releases, wholesale prices rose up to 25% and outages increased by 0.5-1 a year near data centers Golden et al. (2026).
  • Host school districts' property-tax revenue rose 16.6%, a quasi-experimental estimate that fails multiple-testing correction Bahar and Wright (2026); a state audit finds Virginia's sales-tax exemption saved the industry $928 million in FY23 JLARC staff (2024); subsidy tabulations show the largest megadeals averaging $1.95 million per permanent job Good Jobs First (2025); and incentives equal about 2% of construction investment in hyperscale counties but 62% in colocation counties, where employment gains are smallest Bahar and Wright (2026).
  • Model-based projections rise steeply: US data-center use of 176 TWh in 2023 reaches 325-580 TWh by 2028 across scenarios Shehabi et al. (2024); a dispatch model projects wholesale prices roughly 50% higher by 2028 under high build-out Kay et al. (2026); and a state audit finds unconstrained Virginia electricity demand would double within 10 years and typical residential costs could rise $14-$37 per month in real terms by 2040 JLARC staff (2024).
  • Environmental footprints rest on accounting and projections: global data-center electricity use could double to about 1,065 TWh by 2030 International Energy Agency (2025); US data centers generated about $25 billion in air-pollution and climate damages in 2025 (range $10–$33 billion), 30% in Texas and Virginia Muller (2026); and projected 2030 global footprints reach 9.3 trillion liters of water and 14,500 km² of land Aczel et al. (2026).
  • Gross contribution figures are not causal estimates: an input-output study commissioned by an industry trade association credits the sector with $926.9 billion of US GDP and 5.5 million jobs supported in 2024 PwC (2026), and reports prepared for Google attribute €110 million a year of GDP to its Belgian data center Thelle et al. (2015) and about $1.1 billion a year to its Loudoun County investments Deloitte Consulting LLP (2023).
  • No causal estimate comes from a developing country. Descriptive data show only 52 percent of low-income economies have access to a colocation data center and none has a direct cloud on-ramp Gelvanovska-Garcia et al. (2024). A calibrated trade model finds a 10-percentage-point cost-of-capital gap adds about $0.29 per GPU-hour, roughly four times the electricity-cost spread, so finance, governance and buyer trust, not power prices, bind Lokshin (2026).

Mechanisms

  • Effects concentrate in the facility's own sector and stay local: data-processing employment rises 56% over a decade with wages unchanged Bahar and Wright (2026), and night-time radiance jumps 38-70 percent within 1km of a site but fades beyond 5km Bahar and Wright (2026).
  • Siting shapes who gains: third-party data centers cluster in metropolitan areas (96.4% of host counties) while hyperscalers follow electricity costs Fang and Greenstein (2025), and local job and wage gains appear only in metro counties Yue and Zeng (2026).
  • Large loads can raise costs for other grid users: in an IV design, cryptomining cost Upstate New York households roughly $204 million a year Benetton et al. (2023); in a CGE model, transmission limits drive most of the projected price increase Bogmans et al. (2025).
  • Certificate accounting can mask grid effects: renewable certificates are averaged annually while consumption is real-time, so data centers claiming 100% coverage still degrade reliability; behind-the-meter colocation with storage mitigates more than certificates alone Golden et al. (2026).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Nearly all causal evidence evaluates investment, that is, facility openings; policy reform enters only through subsidy comparisons in Bahar and Wright (2026), and no causal study evaluates adoption and use. Tax exemptions, tariff design and siting rules lack causal evaluation.
  • All causal estimates come from the United States. Developing-country evidence is descriptive or model-based Gelvanovska-Garcia et al. (2024), Lokshin (2026), and local resource pressure in Querétaro (Mexico) and Uruguay appears only as case material Aczel et al. (2026); local jobs, fiscal returns and tariffs there are unmeasured.
  • No causal study covers inclusion or human capital. Water, land and emissions costs rest on accounting and projections, and quasi-experimental retail-price evidence largely ends by 2024 Watten et al. (2026), Garcia-Appendini et al. (2025), before most projected load growth Shehabi et al. (2024).
  • Incentive cost-effectiveness is unmeasured: cost-per-job figures come from subsidy tabulations Good Jobs First (2025), the general-equilibrium analysis is theoretical Johansson and Kriström (2021), and the largest benefit figures are industry-commissioned input-output contributions PwC (2026).

Cloud computing20 studies · 6 causalQuasi-experimental firm studies from the US, UK and France consistently find cloud adoption raises growth, productivity and survival, most for young and small firms DeStefano et al. (2025), Jin and McElheran (2025); comparable magnitudes are scarce, and outside China developing-country evidence is descriptive.

What the evidence shows

  • An IV design using UK fiber-broadband rollout finds cloud adoption raises employment, revenue and productivity growth in young firms, which concentrate activity in fewer establishments; incumbents gain less and restructure, with more establishment closures and fewer openings DeStefano et al. (2025).
  • US Census plant-level evidence shows young manufacturing plants that rent IT as a service survive and grow more, while owning IT capital is associated with higher failure among young plants; productivity returns to IT services are higher for young plants than for older incumbents Jin and McElheran (2025).
  • French firm panels show cloud adoption raises long-run size growth, with smaller firms gaining more than larger ones Caldarola and Fontanelli (2024). In China, exposure-design estimates show industries more exposed to falling cloud costs see more entry, exit and M&A and lower concentration, whereas AI exposure raises concentration and favors larger firms Lu et al. (2024).
  • Policy can slow diffusion: in a quasi-natural experiment, a UK capital-allowance incentive raised owned IT investment but slowed adoption of cloud, big data and AI, which substitute for owned capital, and cut firms' demand for data-analytics workers DeStefano et al. (2024).
  • A staggered difference-in-differences links US cloud adoption to 6.9% higher long-term sales and 2.24% higher productivity Jin and Bai (2022); a structural learning model on CPU-utilization data for nearly 100,000 firms finds their productivity in using cloud rises 33% in the first year, stabilizing after four years Brand et al. (2025); and an AWS-funded cross-country regression associates 1% higher cloud penetration with 0.31% higher labor productivity Katz and Jung (2024).
  • Survey evidence shows who adopts: in 2018 about 25% of US firms used cloud for all IT functions, with young small firms ahead of old ones (74% versus 58%) Foster et al. (2021); adoption among Italian firms rose from 28% in 2020 to over 50% in early 2024, correlated with size and exporting Bencivelli et al. (2025); and in developing countries cloud adoption is sharply skewed toward larger firms Cirera et al. (2022).
  • Economy-wide effects come only from models and correlations: a DSGE simulation projects cloud adding up to 0.3% to annual EU growth under fast adoption Etro (2009), and a CGE model estimates data-localization rules cut GDP by 0.1% to 1.7% across seven economies Bauer et al. (2014). Access is unequal: no low-income country has a direct cloud on-ramp to a hyperscaler Gelvanovska-Garcia et al. (2024).

Mechanisms

  • Renting replaces fixed IT investment, lowering barriers for young and small firms: young plants renting IT as a service survive more often than those owning IT capital Jin and McElheran (2025), and smaller French firms gain more growth Caldarola and Fontanelli (2024).
  • Learning by using: firms' productivity in using cloud rises 33% in the first year and stabilizes only after four years, with gains staying within divisions and little transfer across divisions of the same firm Brand et al. (2025).
  • Cloud enables reorganization: young firms concentrate activity in fewer establishments, incumbents close more and open fewer, and both disperse remaining establishments farther from headquarters DeStefano et al. (2025); cloud exposure also raises equity and venture financing Lu et al. (2024).
  • Owned IT and cloud are substitutes, so subsidizing owned capital slowed cloud adoption DeStefano et al. (2024); cloud adoption follows fiber broadband rollout, which the UK IV design exploits DeStefano et al. (2025), and correlational OECD-country estimates tie cloud gains to broadband Katz and Jung (2024).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Most causal evidence concerns firms' adoption and use; policy reform is limited to a UK capital-allowance incentive DeStefano et al. (2024), and no causal study evaluates public investment or programs, such as government cloud migration, shared data infrastructure or adoption support.
  • Apart from China, no causal study covers a developing country; evidence there is correlational survey data Cirera et al. (2022) and infrastructure mapping Gelvanovska-Garcia et al. (2024), so effects for small firms in low-income settings, where hyperscaler on-ramps are absent, are unknown.
  • No causal study measures household welfare, inclusion or environmental outcomes, and wage effects on workers are unmeasured; environmental evidence comes only from accounting of data-center and digital-sector emissions Muller (2026), Axenbeck et al. (2026).
  • No study reports firms' adoption costs or the cost-effectiveness of cloud programs; economy-wide gains rest on a DSGE simulation Etro (2009), official statistics understate cloud investment Byrne et al. (2018), and localization effects are modeled at the GDP level Bauer et al. (2014), not measured for cloud use.
Policy reform5Investment & programs5Adoption & use12
Digital public infrastructure18 studies · 12 causalRandomized trials, mostly from India, solidly show that biometric ID and authenticated payments cut leakage, by 41% in one workfare program Muralidharan et al. (2016), but poorly managed authentication mandates also exclude: 1.5-2 million eligible beneficiaries temporarily lost subsidized food Muralidharan et al. (2025).

What the evidence shows

  • Randomized evidence shows biometric Smartcard payments in Andhra Pradesh cut leakage by 41% in workfare and 47% in pensions while paying beneficiaries 6-10 days sooner, with 22 fewer minutes spent collecting and no reduction in access Muralidharan et al. (2016). Quasi-experimental estimates find Aadhaar- and bank-verified transfers for cooking-gas subsidies cut subsidized fuel purchases by 11-14%, consistent with removing ghost accounts Barnwal (2017).
  • Randomized and natural-experiment evidence finds compulsory biometric authentication for India's food rations reduced corruption but left 1.5-2 million eligible beneficiaries temporarily without subsidized food, mostly through abrupt cutovers and connectivity and seeding failures Muralidharan et al. (2025). A descriptive survey in Jharkhand found exclusion errors of about 20% where every ration sale required authentication, falling hardest on the elderly and manual laborers Drèze et al. (2017).
  • Gains extend to frontline services but not always to fraud. In a cluster-randomized trial, biometric devices in Indian tuberculosis centers made patients 25% less likely to interrupt treatment and reduced overreporting of patient numbers Bossuroy et al. (2025). Quasi-experimental evidence finds Afghanistan's biometric, mobile-money teacher payroll cut salary delays and improved educational outcomes but did not reduce payments to ghost workers Blumenstock et al. (2023).
  • In the randomized Smartcard rollout, beneficiary household earnings rose 14% and poverty fell 26%, with 86% of the income gain coming from non-program earnings as private-sector wages and employment rose Muralidharan et al. (2023). Depositing workfare wages into women's own accounts, with training, raised their public- and private-sector work by 0.19 and 0.17 standard deviations in a randomized trial and shifted gender norms Field et al. (2021).
  • Quasi-experimental estimates for Pakistan's national cash-transfer program find biometric verification at retail agents raised the likelihood that women collected cash themselves by 46 percentage points, without significantly changing the net amount received Clark and Vyborny (2022). Descriptive survey data suggest Aadhaar-enabled accounts raised ownership among women and poor adults, though informal costs of opening an account remain larger for women, rural residents and less-educated people Demirguc-Kunt et al. (2017).
  • Quasi-experimental estimates from India find an interoperability mandate raised peer-to-merchant payments per person by 8.3 rupees per month more in more fragmented districts, 93% of their pre-integration mean; model-based aggregation puts the national rise in digital-payment use at over 50% Copestake et al. (2025). Districts whose lead bank joined UPI early had 7.5% higher household income in a draft not yet peer reviewed Dubey and Purnanandam (2023).
  • In credit markets, a Malawi randomized trial found fingerprinting borrowers raised repayment among the highest-risk borrowers, with a benefit-cost ratio of 2.34 Giné et al. (2012). Quasi-experimental open-banking evidence is early: after countries adopt open-banking rules, VC-backed fintech financings rise by about a third, but UK gains from new, cheaper non-bank lending went mainly to SMEs with prior lending relationships Babina et al. (2025).

Mechanisms

  • Verification removes ghost beneficiaries whose subsidies feed black markets: when India's verified cooking-gas transfer policy was unexpectedly ended, black-market fuel prices fell by 13-20% as diverted subsidized fuel flowed back Barnwal (2017).
  • Paying women directly displaces intermediaries: biometric collection raised the probability that women decide how finances are used by 9 percentage points among those who had relied on intermediaries Clark and Vyborny (2022); own-account wage deposits raised women's independent banking Field et al. (2021).
  • Verified identity and payment data ease credit frictions: fingerprinting let a lender deny defaulters new loans under new identities, raising repayment Giné et al. (2012), and lending likely based on payment data accelerated in districts more fragmented before UPI interoperability Copestake et al. (2025).
  • Exclusion stems mainly from how transitions are managed: ration losses followed abrupt cutovers and connectivity and seeding failures Muralidharan et al. (2025), and failed fingerprint matches, poor connectivity and incomplete seeding hit the elderly and manual laborers hardest Drèze et al. (2017).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Most causal evidence evaluates public programs and investments, chiefly India's biometric payment rollouts; fewer causal studies evaluate policy and regulatory reform such as authentication mandates, interoperability rules and open banking, and very few examine adoption and use by people or firms.
  • E-signature has no study, and data-exchange platforms, property-registry interoperability and corporate digital ID have only descriptive or conceptual work Deininger et al. (2025), Leung et al. (2022); no causal study covers environment or resilience, and growth and labor-market effects come only from trials within India's workfare program.
  • Causal evidence comes almost entirely from South Asia: outside cross-country open-banking work, Africa has only an older credit trial Giné et al. (2012), Latin America and the Middle East have no causal country study, and cross-country evidence on pandemic transfers is descriptive Marin and Palacios (2022).
  • Costs are rarely measured: beyond a benefit-cost ratio for borrower fingerprinting Giné et al. (2012) and fiscal-savings estimates for Smartcards Muralidharan et al. (2016), there is no cost-effectiveness evidence on building ID, authentication or interoperable payment systems, little long-run evidence, and no causal study of privacy safeguards.
Policy reform7Investment & programs16Adoption & use2
Digital government platforms & services54 studies · 35 causalRandomized and quasi-experimental evidence is fairly solid that digital tax, payment and monitoring systems raise compliance and cut leakage; e-filing doubled taxes paid by high-evasion firms Okunogbe and Pouliquen (2022). Gains depend on enforcement and can reverse: land-record digitization in Pakistan cut tax collection by 47% Aman-Rana and Minaudier (2026).

What the evidence shows

  • In Ghana, a randomized trial of a tool that helps collectors locate property owners raised bill deliveries by 27% and property-tax collections by 103% Dzansi et al. (2024). Quasi-experimental evidence from Tajikistan's e-filing rollout shows it cut firms' tax-compliance time by 40% and doubled taxes paid by firms more likely to evade, while others paid less tax and fewer bribes Okunogbe and Pouliquen (2022).
  • Quasi-experimental estimates vary with design: reported sales, purchases and VAT liabilities rose more than 5% in Peru's first year of e-invoicing, mostly among small firms Bellon et al. (2022); reported VAT liabilities rose nearly 150% when larger Ugandan firms had to integrate directly with the tax authority Lees et al. (2025); and Pakistan's real-time risk checks on VAT credits raised country-level net VAT collection at least 10% Shah (2026).
  • Quasi-experimental studies also find nulls and reversals. Uruguay's VAT rebates for card payments raised card transactions 50% but had a near-zero effect on firms' reported sales and VAT liabilities Brockmeyer and Somarriba (2025); Ugandan firms cut reported sales 39% after e-invoicing integration, suggesting sales suppression Lees et al. (2025); and Pakistan's land-record digitization cut agricultural tax collection 47% without shrinking the tax base, as officials lost leverage Aman-Rana and Minaudier (2026).
  • Procurement evidence is quasi-experimental and mixed on prices. Bangladesh's e-procurement added 1.6-2.2 bidders, cut single-bidder probability by 7.8-13.5 percentage points and raised winning discounts by 7.4-8.0 percentage points Blum et al. (2023). In road contracts, e-procurement did not lower prices but drew in outside contractors, improving quality in India and cutting delays in Indonesia Lewis-Faupel et al. (2016); electronic auctions raised Ukraine's public land-lease revenue 175% Deininger et al. (2023).
  • Randomized trials in India find digital controls cut leakage, sometimes at beneficiaries' expense. E-invoicing-triggered fund release cut workfare spending 24% and officials' personal wealth 10% but lengthened payment delays Banerjee et al. (2020); announced phone checks with beneficiaries cut non-receipt of farm-input transfers by 7.6% at 3.6 cents per extra dollar delivered Muralidharan et al. (2021); biometric ration authentication reduced corruption but temporarily excluded 1.5-2 million eligible beneficiaries Muralidharan et al. (2025).
  • Information tools raise bureaucratic efficiency in randomized trials. Giving Indian officials a dashboard of pending workfare payments sped processing by 17% (1.4 days) and raised household days worked by 10%, with benefits estimated at more than 170 times costs Dodge et al. (2025). Biometric tracking in tuberculosis centers raised health-worker attendance and made patients 25% less likely to interrupt treatment Bossuroy et al. (2025).
  • Quasi-experimental estimates find Pakistan's land-record digitization expanded agricultural lending by PKR 5-7 billion, mostly to the smallest borrowers, and roughly tripled recorded corruption cases, which the author attributes to better detection Hussain (2026); India's registry computerization raised urban mortgage credit modestly, with no detectable rural effect Deininger and Goyal (2012). In Senegal, a randomized trial found bureaucrats' discretionary valuations undervalued high-value properties, making taxes regressive Knebelmann et al. (2023).

Mechanisms

  • Digital paper trails make enforcement credible: audit-threat letters had much larger effects on reported sales where no cross-verifiable trail existed Pomeranz (2015), and in Rwanda most of e-invoicing's compliance gain came from audits becoming more deterrent Kotsogiannis et al. (2025).
  • Enlisting third parties adds verifiable information: lottery rewards for requesting receipts raised firms' reported sales at least 21% and net tax revenue 9.3% Naritomi (2019), and letting workers verify employer wage reports raised reported wages at underreporting firms Kumler et al. (2020).
  • Removing face-to-face discretion cuts extortion but also officials' leverage: e-filing reduced bribes, consistent with officials having treated firms differently Okunogbe and Pouliquen (2022), while land-record digitization lowered collection as revenue officials lost influence over taxpayers Aman-Rana and Minaudier (2026).
  • Cheaper information lets managers act: a payment-tracking dashboard worked because managers' cost of acquiring information was the binding constraint Dodge et al. (2025), and announcing phone checks with beneficiaries cut non-delivery by frontline officials Muralidharan et al. (2021).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Most causal evidence evaluates investments and programs, with a substantial share evaluating mandates and regulatory reforms, mostly in tax administration; only a few causal studies examine how officials, firms or citizens adopt and use these systems, and none covers environment and resilience.
  • One-stop citizen portals, financial management information systems and participatory platforms have only descriptive evidence Jordan SANAD portal (2022), Cambodia FMIS reform (2023), Nigeria participatory budgeting platforms (2024), so causal estimates of their effects on access, time costs and trust are missing.
  • E-procurement has no randomized evaluation, and studies mostly measure tendering rather than contract execution, where rent-seeking may have moved; Bangladesh's savings and GDP gains are extrapolations Blum et al. (2023), and Ukraine's ProZorro estimates lack a control group Kovalchuk et al. (2019).
  • Long-run effects and costs are rarely measured: most estimates cover only the first years after rollout, though firms shift to other evasion margins Lees et al. (2025); cost-effectiveness is reported for few tools Muralidharan et al. (2021), Dodge et al. (2025); and no causal study covers the Middle East.
Policy reform22Investment & programs49Adoption & use8
Digital payments & mobile money48 studies · 35 causalQuasi-experimental and randomized studies consistently show that mobile money lets users absorb shocks that cut non-users' consumption 7% Jack and Suri (2014) and gives women more financial control Heath and Riley (2024); effects on poverty and firm profits are mixed, and fast-payment evidence is recent.

What the evidence shows

  • Quasi-experimental studies in East Africa find mobile money extends risk sharing: in Kenya, shocks cut non-users' consumption by 7% while users' consumption was unaffected Jack and Suri (2014), and in Tanzania users smoothed village rainfall shocks that cut non-users' consumption Riley (2018). A Mozambique randomized trial found mobile money raised remittances and welfare, especially during floods and other shocks, but also out-migration and lower farm investment Batista and Vicente (2023).
  • Quasi-experimental estimates find M-Pesa access lifted an estimated 194,000 Kenyan households out of extreme poverty, more so for female-headed households Suri and Jack (2016). In randomized trials, Indonesia's switch to e-vouchers delivered 46% more aid and cut poverty 20% for the poorest 15% Banerjee et al. (2023), but Ghana's mobile-money pandemic transfers raised income 20% only while paid, with negative consumption effects two years later Karlan et al. (2026).
  • In randomized trials, Ugandan women whose business loans came by mobile money rather than cash had about 11% more business capital and 15% higher profits Riley (2024); repaying microfinance loans by mobile money raised Tanzanian women's control over finances by 0.37 standard deviations Heath and Riley (2024); and mobile rather than cash transfers in Niger raised dietary diversity 9%-16% and women's control over spending Aker et al. (2016).
  • In a Kenyan randomized trial, offering merchants e-payment accounts raised mobile-loan access by at least 50% (0.17 SD) but had no effect on sales or profits Dalton et al. (2024). Quasi-experimental studies find small retailers that adopted card terminals in Mexico gained sales and profits Higgins (2024), and Pix raised employment in micro establishments by 1.7% per standard deviation of prior mobile penetration, narrowing wage inequality Burga et al. (2026).
  • Quasi-experimental studies find fast payments widen access to finance: a 1% rise in active Pix users raised first-time bank-account holders by 0.80% Sampaio and Ornelas (2024), and fintech lending to new-to-credit borrowers grew 45-fold with 5.3% lower default rates in India's high-UPI-exposure areas Alok et al. (2024). A review reports risks: 62% of Malawian digital borrowers failed to repay on time, and providers had misled them about late fees J-PAL (2025).
  • Randomized entry of mobile-money agents in Ghana cut vendor misconduct 46% and markups on non-financial goods 32% Annan (2025). In Brazil, fintech competition exposure, facilitated by Pix and open finance, is associated with 3.7 percentage points lower bank lending rates per standard deviation IMF staff (2026), and a doubling of Pix transaction value with a 14-basis-point narrowing of the small-large bank deposit-rate gap Sarkisyan (2026).
  • After Uganda's 2018 tax of 1% on transactions, revised to 0.5% on withdrawals, difference-in-differences estimates show users in high-ATM-density districts transacted 4% to 12% less than others, while rural users had fewer substitutes Spadavecchia et al. (2025). A triple-difference finds rural food consumption fell 10-18% after Tanzania's levy raised the fee on a USD 18 transfer by 140%, though several estimates are statistically insignificant Paul and Sharma (2025).

Mechanisms

  • Cheaper transfers widen risk-sharing networks: Kenyan users' consumption held up after shocks because they received more remittances from more diverse senders Jack and Suri (2014), and Tanzanian users drew on distant networks against village-wide rainfall shocks Riley (2018).
  • Privacy shifts control: mobile-money loans raised women's business capital because funds were shielded from household members' claims, most for women facing the strongest pressure to share Riley (2024); less visible mobile transfers were harder for others to claim Aker et al. (2016).
  • Payment records substitute for credit histories: merchant e-payment accounts raised mobile borrowing, plausibly by reducing information asymmetries Dalton et al. (2024), and UPI-driven digital footprints let fintechs lend to new-to-credit borrowers without higher defaults Alok et al. (2024).
  • Network effects and interoperability drive use: government debit cards led retailers to adopt terminals, raising other consumers' card adoption 21% Higgins (2024), and a structural model finds ending wallets' POS-terminal interoperability would cut wallet usage 26.01 percentage points Andia et al. (2026).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Most causal evidence evaluates investments and programs, from transfer delivery to agent networks, followed by household and firm adoption of mobile money; policy and regulatory reform, such as mobile-money taxes, interoperability mandates and open banking, has the fewest causal studies, all recent.
  • Fraud and consumer protection are thinly covered: a randomized test found standard scam-detection tips did not help users spot scams Kubilay et al. (2023), fraud trends are documented only descriptively Khiaonarong and Zheng (2026), and no study evaluates consumer-protection or dispute-resolution rules.
  • Growth, labor-market, human-capital and environmental outcomes have very few causal studies; Pix's labor-market evidence covers formal jobs only Burga et al. (2026), long-run follow-ups are rare, and in Ghana transfer gains did not persist Karlan et al. (2026).
  • Causal evidence on fast payment systems comes almost entirely from Pix and UPI, no causal study focuses on the Middle East and North Africa, and cost data are rare beyond transfer delivery, such as under 7 cents per dollar in Afghanistan Callen et al. (2025).

Digital skills52 studies · 25 causalRandomized trials find digital skills training alone seldom raises earnings or employment; combined with a job-referral guarantee it lifted earnings 37% Atkin et al. (2024), and edtech with on-site support raised math achievement almost half a standard deviation Oreopoulos et al. (2026). Evidence is experimental and solid but mostly short-run.

What the evidence shows

  • Randomized trials find skills training alone does not improve labor-market or business outcomes: digital skills training did not raise Nairobi youth's earnings or employment Atkin et al. (2024), e-commerce training did not raise Georgian firms' digital participation Coville et al. (2026), freelance training did not raise East African trainees' online work or earnings Charles et al. (2026), and app-based training had 22% completion versus 71% in person, with negligible effects either way Cassidy et al. (2024).
  • Randomized arms that addressed demand or job matching did better. Training combined with a job-referral guarantee raised monthly earnings by 37% (women 60%, men 26%) and cut unemployment by 10 percentage points Atkin et al. (2024). A conditional purchase order raised Georgian firms' online market access by 24 percentage points, though effects largely dissipated as control firms caught up Coville et al. (2026).
  • Meta-analytic evidence sets a modest benchmark: across active labor market RCTs, vocational training raises earnings by a median 7.7%, only about one-third of all estimates are positive and significant, and coaching, incentives and sector targeting are associated with larger training effects Yeyati et al. (2025). A review finds most recent Sub-Saharan African skills-training trials improve employment, partly owing to better-targeted, market-linked designs Beber et al. (2025).
  • Randomized tutoring trials show sizable learning gains: adaptive software raised math and Hindi scores by 0.37 and 0.23 SD in 4.5 months, most for students furthest behind Muralidharan et al. (2019); a WhatsApp AI math tutor in Ghana had a 0.37 effect size after a school year Henkel et al. (2024); and a six-week chatbot pilot in one Nigerian school raised learning about 0.3 SD, more for girls De Simone et al. (2025).
  • In randomized trials, implementation decides results: on-site support raised Khan Academy use from 7.2 to 47.4 minutes per week and math achievement by almost 0.5 SD Oreopoulos et al. (2026); Nigerian girls' digital literacy index rose nearly 10% where classes were implemented, with no significant pooled effect Chang et al. (2026); unrestricted chatbot access cut Turkish students' unassisted exam scores 17%, while a safeguarded tutor avoided harm without gains Bastani et al. (2025).
  • Returns to digital skills are positive, larger in poorer countries, and mostly correlational. Instrumental-variable estimates exploiting broadband rollout find a one standard deviation increase in ICT skills raises wages by 23.6% in Germany Falck et al. (2021). In descriptive job-posting data from 29 countries, requiring at least one digital skill carries a 7.5% advertised wage premium in low- and middle-income countries versus 1.3% in high-income countries Liu et al. (2026).
  • Experimental evidence on generative AI at work shows larger gains for less-experienced workers: Copilot access raised developers' completed tasks by 26.08%, more for less-experienced developers Cui et al. (2025), and quasi-experimental evidence finds an AI dispatch tool narrowed the taxi-driver productivity gap by 14% Kanazawa et al. (2022). Outside the AI's capability frontier, consultants using AI were 19% less likely to produce correct solutions Dell'Acqua et al. (2025).

Mechanisms

  • Non-skill barriers bind: freelance trainees created Upwork profiles but found no more work, which the authors attribute to payment, identity-verification and reputation barriers Charles et al. (2026); Georgian firms went online when offered a buyer, not when trained Coville et al. (2026).
  • Matching matters: training raised earnings only with a job-referral guarantee Atkin et al. (2024); firm-based training worked mainly through better screening of worker ability Alfonsi et al. (2020); job-search advice gains eroded at high saturation as job seekers competed for the same vacancies Altmann et al. (2022).
  • Sustained, structured use drives learning: on-site support raised weekly Khan Academy use from 7.2 to 47.4 minutes Oreopoulos et al. (2026), adaptive software helped students furthest behind most Muralidharan et al. (2019), and unrestricted chatbots invited copying Bastani et al. (2025).
  • Returns run partly through job sorting: selection into abstract-task occupations explains two-thirds of the ICT-skill wage gain Falck et al. (2021); AI tools substitute for missing experience, so less-experienced developers gain more Cui et al. (2025).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Causal evidence splits between investment and public programs, such as training and tutoring, and the adoption and use of digital and AI tools; policy and regulatory reform is almost untested, and a US school internet subsidy found no significant effect on student performance Goolsbee and Guryan (2006).
  • No causal study covers economic growth, public sector effectiveness or environment; growth claims rest on macro-model projections of 0.1% to 0.3% higher long-run GDP from e-skills reforms Lorenzani and Varga (2014) and cross-country correlations Magoutas et al. (2024).
  • Follow-ups are short: AI-tutoring trials run from six weeks De Simone et al. (2025) to one school year Henkel et al. (2024), so persistence is unknown. Few trials report costs, so cost-effectiveness cannot be compared; model-based costing puts the global digital-skills gap at about $152 billion International Telecommunication Union (2025).
  • Settings are narrow: generative-AI workplace trials come mostly from the United States and multinational firms, developing East Asia has no causal study, and Latin American causal evidence is a coding-bootcamp trial whose public summary emphasizes design lessons over impact estimates World Bank (2018).
Policy reform3Investment & programs32Adoption & use29
Broader digital transformation80 studies · 38 causalExperiments show digital platforms cut trade costs, by roughly one-fifth in Ugandan agricultural markets Bergquist et al. (2026), but rural e-commerce raised little income for producers Couture et al. (2021). Causal micro evidence is solid but gains are uneven; growth evidence is only correlational or model-based.

What the evidence shows

  • A randomized rollout of an SMS trading platform in Uganda cut fixed trade costs by roughly one-fifth, raised trade between treated markets about 7% (1% market-wide) and narrowed maize price dispersion about 6-11%, mostly benefiting larger traders though farmgate prices rose up to 12% in previously low-price markets Bergquist et al. (2026). Gravity comparisons find the distance effect 65% smaller on eBay than in total trade Lendle et al. (2016).
  • A randomized rural e-commerce program in China raised little income for producers or workers; gains came from lower living costs for a minority of younger, richer households in remote markets Couture et al. (2021). Structural estimates put China's average welfare gain at 1.6%, about 30% larger for the smallest cities Fan et al. (2018); quasi-experimental US card data show larger gains for higher-income consumers and denser counties Dolfen et al. (2023).
  • In Georgia, a randomized conditional purchase order raised small firms' online market access by 24 percentage points, fading as controls caught up, while e-commerce training failed to raise participation Coville et al. (2026); a randomized rollout of a seller dashboard raised eBay weekly sales 3.6% Bar-Gill et al. (2023). Structural production-function estimates find a business website raises TFP for 54.6% of developing-country manufacturers, with a median premium of 2.2% Cusolito et al. (2020).
  • Platform results are mixed. Paid advertising plus applicant identity verification on an Indian job portal raised hiring by 68% in a field experiment Kelley and coauthors (2023), but randomized freelance training in East Africa had no significant effect on online work or earnings Charles et al. (2026). A difference-in-differences finds posts for automation-prone writing and coding jobs fell 21% relative to manual-intensive jobs within eight months of ChatGPT Demirci et al. (2025).
  • Working from home raised call-center performance 13% in a randomized trial in China, rising to 22% when workers could choose, though promotion rates conditional on performance fell Bloom et al. (2015). Descriptive data show platform drivers in India, Indonesia and Kenya out-earn low-skill jobs monthly by working longer, with comparable or lower hourly net earnings, and Kenyan drivers often exit involuntarily Adhvaryu et al. (2026).
  • Mobile money shows consistent welfare and gender gains. Quasi-experimental estimates find M-Pesa access lifted roughly 2% of Kenyan households out of extreme poverty, with a 9.2% reduction among female-headed households Suri and Jack (2016); a randomized introduction in rural Mozambique raised remittances and welfare, especially after floods, while increasing out-migration and lowering farm activity Batista and Vicente (2023).
  • Unlike the micro evidence, growth evidence is correlational or model-based: technology sophistication correlates 0.87 with labor productivity across 44 regions, which the authors say cannot be read causally Cirera et al. (2022), and trade-model scenarios project AI raising global GDP 12 to 13% by 2040, with low-income economies' incomes rising 8% versus 14% for high-income ones if they do not catch up digitally World Trade Organization (2025).

Mechanisms

  • Lower search costs integrate markets: once mobile coverage arrived, the share of Kerala fishermen selling outside their home market rose from zero to about 35% Jensen (2007), and an SMS platform let larger traders arbitrage across Ugandan markets Bergquist et al. (2026).
  • Verification and reputation ease information frictions: identity verification with paid advertising raised job-portal hiring Kelley and coauthors (2023), seller ratings further shrink distance effects on eBay Lendle et al. (2016), and generative AI erased the hiring premium for tailored freelance proposals Galdin and Silbert (2025).
  • Insurance channel: shocks cut non-users' consumption 7 percent but not M-Pesa users', via remittances Jack and Suri (2014), and firms in industries one standard deviation more digitalized had about 4 percent smaller sales declines one year into the COVID recession Copestake et al. (2022).
  • Network effects and complements spread adoption: government debit cards led retailers to adopt terminals, raising other consumers' card adoption by 21% Higgins (2024), and UPI-linked credit grew most where low-cost internet and bank accounts were both present Alok et al. (2024).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Causal evidence covers technology adoption and use most, then investment and public programs such as platform rollouts and mobile money; policy and regulatory reform is almost untested, and a free mobile-data trial in Kenya found no significant change in employment or consumption Suri and Bhattacharya (2022).
  • Public sector effectiveness and environment have almost no causal study: environmental figures are input-output or model estimates, such as digital industries' share of about 4.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions Axenbeck et al. (2026), and no study credibly estimates aggregate GDP effects.
  • Remote-work causal evidence comes only from the United States and China, platform and e-commerce trials cover a handful of countries, the Middle East and North Africa has no causal study, and long-run evidence such as M-Pesa's Suri and Jack (2016) is rare.
  • Cost data are nearly absent: no causal study reports cost per beneficiary, so platform, e-commerce and firm digitalization programs cannot be ranked on value for money; in Georgia, a purchase offer six times larger added only a modest increase Coville et al. (2026).
Policy reform9Investment & programs27Adoption & use63
Artificial intelligence145 studies · 53 causalExperiments and quasi-experiments show generative AI raises productivity on suitable tasks, 14% for call-center agents and most for novices Brynjolfsson et al. (2025), but not beyond its frontier Dell'Acqua et al. (2025). Entry-level hiring in exposed jobs has weakened Brynjolfsson et al. (2026); aggregate employment effects remain undetectable Gimbel et al. (2026); macroeconomic gains are projections.

What the evidence shows

  • Randomized trials find large gains on well-defined tasks: ChatGPT cut completion time on writing tasks 40% and raised quality 18% Noy and Zhang (2023), and Copilot raised developers' completed tasks 26.1%, more for less-experienced developers Cui et al. (2025). Gains have limits: consultants using AI were 19% less likely to solve a task beyond its frontier correctly Dell'Acqua et al. (2025), and AI made experienced open-source developers 19% slower Becker et al. (2025).
  • Early-career workers show the first labor-market effects. Employment of 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed US occupations is 19% below the path of less-exposed peers, with no gap for experienced workers, a descriptive finding Brynjolfsson et al. (2026); quasi-experimental estimates find junior employment about 9% lower at adopting firms after six quarters Hosseini and Lichtinger (2026) and a 1.9 percentage point lower junior share at adopting multinational affiliates Chandar and Teeselink (2026).
  • Aggregate effects are small. Danish data rule out earnings or hours effects above 2% Humlum and Vestergaard (2025), and US difference-in-differences finds no significant employment or wage effect Gimbel et al. (2026), though the 10th-to-90th exposure percentile gap is associated with 4.9% lower median wages Azar et al. (2026). Postings for more AI-substitutable occupations fell a relative 12% in the US Liu et al. (2025) and 5.8% in high-income countries but an insignificant 1.5% elsewhere Huang et al. (2026).
  • Developing-country trials are mixed. A GPT-4 business mentor had no average effect on Kenyan firms, with low performers nearly 10% worse and high performers possibly over 15% better Otis et al. (2026); an OpenAI-funded tool cut Kenyan clinicians' diagnostic errors 16.0% Korom et al. (2025), but another found no significant fall in 14-day treatment failure Agweyu et al. (2026); a WhatsApp AI tutor raised Ghanaian math scores 0.37 SD Henkel et al. (2024).
  • Firm-level quasi-experimental estimates find productivity gains: AI adoption raised EU firms' labor productivity 4% with no adverse employment effect Aldasoro et al. (2026) and Italian firms' value added per employee about 5.2% Ropele and Tagliabracci (2026). Adjustment can be costly: US manufacturing plants show a J-curve of early TFP losses McElheran et al. (2025), and employment at Danish adopters with fewer than 100 employees fell about 16 log points below trend Bonin et al. (2026).
  • Macroeconomic effects are model-based and wide-ranging: projected US TFP gains of 0.66% over ten years Acemoglu (2025), US GDP 1.5% higher by 2035 Penn Wharton Budget Model (2025), 1.6% to 32.4% higher by 2030 across scenarios Korinek et al. (2026), and Poland's GDP 1.3% to 12.1% above baseline by 2035 World Bank Group (2026). The spread reflects assumed exposure, adoption speed and new tasks; advanced economies gain over twice as much as low-income countries Cerutti et al. (2025).
  • Adoption is uneven: Microsoft estimates generative AI use at 27.5% of the working-age population in the Global North versus 15.4% in the Global South Microsoft AI Economy Institute (2026), and a gender gap appears in nearly all regions and occupations Otis et al. (2024). Gains may accrue to capital: in an extreme US scenario the labor share falls from 60% to 45.2% Korinek et al. (2026), and Poland's gains go almost entirely to capital World Bank Group (2026).

Mechanisms

  • AI diffuses expertise and compresses skill gaps: call-center gains concentrated among novices, consistent with AI spreading top performers' practices Brynjolfsson et al. (2025), and less-experienced developers gained more, consistent with AI substituting for missing experience Cui et al. (2025).
  • Entry-level tasks are substituted first: junior employment falls through slower hiring while senior employment rises at adopting firms Hosseini and Lichtinger (2026), Chandar and Teeselink (2026), and the divergence concentrates where AI use substitutes for rather than complements workers Brynjolfsson et al. (2026).
  • Outcomes depend on users' judgment and guardrails: Kenyan entrepreneurs' results diverged with the AI advice they chose to implement Otis et al. (2026), and students using unrestricted GPT-4 copied answers and scored 17% lower unassisted, while a safeguarded tutor avoided that harm Bastani et al. (2025).
  • Adoption spreads through expectations and complements: correcting firms' underestimates of peers' AI investment raised their own planned investment Baumann et al. (2026), gains require complementary investment in software, data and training Aldasoro et al. (2026), and early adopters face adjustment costs McElheran et al. (2025).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Nearly all causal evidence concerns technology adoption and use; investment and public programs appear mainly in education, health and business-advice trials, and policy and regulatory reform is almost unevaluated, with one event study of the EU AI Act measuring only shareholder value Chen et al. (2026).
  • Developing-country evidence is thin: a handful of trials in Kenya, Ghana and Nigeria, early wage effects for young Brazilian workers Aguirre and Meloni (2026) and posting data Huang et al. (2026). A farm-advisory chatbot trial has no results yet Abate et al. (2025); agricultural and public-service applications remain largely untested.
  • Long-run and general-equilibrium effects are unknown: most trials last weeks or months, labor-market studies cover about three years since ChatGPT, and one investment-based model implies 5 to 58 percentage points of cumulative US GDP growth by 2030 Wachter and Wachter (2026).
  • Costs and side effects are rarely measured: few studies report cost-effectiveness, though one Kenyan clinical tool cost US$0.04 per patient Agweyu et al. (2026); environmental costs rest on projections such as 8.6% higher US electricity prices Bogmans et al. (2025); and distributional effects within developing countries lack causal evidence.
Policy reform10Investment & programs32Adoption & use132
Social media15 studies · 11 causalRandomized trials find social media use modestly raises political participation, with effects on polarization and turnout close to zero Allcott et al. (2024); accuracy nudges cut intentions to share misinformation by 4.9% in Kenya and Nigeria Offer-Westort et al. (2024). Evidence is experimental but mostly US-based and short-run.

What the evidence shows

  • In a large randomized trial, deactivating Facebook for six weeks before the 2020 US election cut a political participation index by 0.167 SD, mostly online participation, and news knowledge by 0.098 SD; polarization and turnout effects were close to zero Allcott et al. (2024). An earlier randomized four-week deactivation before the 2018 midterms did reduce polarization Allcott et al. (2020); the trials differ in election, duration and sample size.
  • In a randomized trial, X's algorithm made news-organization posts 58.1% less likely to appear, and switching it on for about 7 weeks raised engagement by 0.14 SD and moved policy and current-events attitudes 0.12 SD toward conservative positions, with no significant effect on affective polarization Gauthier et al. (2026). Randomly offering Facebook users subscriptions to counter-attitudinal news outlets modestly reduced negative attitudes toward the opposing party Levy (2021).
  • Mental-health evidence points to harm: Facebook's staggered arrival at US colleges raised the share of students screening positive for severe depression and anxiety, most for those exposed to upward social comparisons, in a quasi-experimental design Braghieri et al. (2022); a randomized four-week deactivation raised subjective well-being Allcott et al. (2020), though switching off WhatsApp media downloads in Brazil, a narrower intervention, did not change well-being Ventura et al. (2025).
  • In Brazil, a randomized trial with more than 700 WhatsApp users found that switching off automatic media downloads before the 2022 election cut recall of false rumors by 0.38 SD but had no significant effect on belief accuracy or polarization; heavy consumers of political content got better at spotting false rumors, while those rarely receiving political news got worse Ventura et al. (2025).
  • Online randomized experiments find modest effects on stated intentions: in Kenya and Nigeria, accuracy nudges cut intentions to share misinformation by 4.9%, while warning flags and related-article suggestions had precisely estimated null effects Offer-Westort et al. (2024); in Jordan, a comprehensive WhatsApp chatbot game raised misinformation discernment by 0.29 SD and cut sharing of misleading headlines by 0.30 SD, but infographics did not improve discernment Dugas et al. (2024).
  • Quasi-experimental studies link social media and misinformation to offline harm: anti-refugee hate crimes in German municipalities with high social media use rose disproportionately when online anti-refugee sentiment was high Müller and Schwarz (2021), and US media markets more exposed to a cable host who downplayed COVID saw less social distancing and higher case and death growth Bursztyn et al. (2023).
  • On regulation, a difference-in-differences finds removing targeted ads from child-directed YouTube content after the 2019 COPPA settlement sharply cut creators' monetization and reshaped kids' content Johnson et al. (2026). Reviews find political effects cut both ways, aiding protest under autocracies but fueling polarization in democracies Zhuravskaya et al. (2020), and connectivity in developing countries can also bring misinformation and lower trust in government Hjort and Tian (2025).

Mechanisms

  • Algorithms change whom users follow: X's algorithm raised following of conservative political-activist accounts by 0.18 SD, which persisted after it was switched off and which the authors use to explain why switching off had no comparable effect Gauthier et al. (2026).
  • Upward social comparison, rather than time displacement, appears to drive the mental-health harm: Facebook's effect on US students' depression and anxiety was larger for those more exposed to upward social comparisons Braghieri et al. (2022).
  • Active prompts work better than passive information: accuracy nudges reduced misinformation-sharing intentions while warning flags did not Offer-Westort et al. (2024), and a chatbot game raised discernment while infographics teaching the same techniques did not Dugas et al. (2024).
  • Social media carries online hostility offline: the link between anti-refugee sentiment on Facebook and hate crimes weakened during local internet or Facebook outages, pointing to a causal role rather than pre-existing local attitudes Müller and Schwarz (2021).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Causal evidence mostly concerns technology adoption and use, through deactivation and feed experiments; a smaller set evaluates programs against misinformation, and policy and regulatory reform is nearly untested beyond a US children's-privacy settlement Johnson et al. (2026), leaving regulation of content moderation and algorithms causally unevaluated.
  • Most causal studies are from the United States; developing-country evidence comes from short experiments in Brazil, Kenya, Nigeria and Jordan, no causal study covers Asia, and mental-health evidence outside the United States is limited to a null well-being result from Brazil Ventura et al. (2025).
  • No causal study covers growth, labor markets or environment; firm effects are limited to YouTube creators under a privacy settlement Johnson et al. (2026), and inclusion has almost no causal evidence, with gender gaps only mapped descriptively from advertising data Breen et al. (2024).
  • Most trials last weeks, not years, and rely mostly on self-reported attitudes or stated sharing intentions rather than observed behavior; none reports costs, so the cost-effectiveness of accuracy nudges or inoculation games at scale is unknown.

Cybersecurity23 studies · 10 causalQuasi-experimental studies show cyber incidents impose large costs: ransomware raises in-hospital mortality 34-38% for patients already admitted Neprash et al. (2026), and a personal-data breach costs the average target 1.1% of market value Kamiya et al. (2021). Evidence on what reduces these costs is thin and mostly descriptive.

What the evidence shows

  • Ransomware harms patients: in Medicare claims, a difference-in-differences design finds patient volume falls 17-24% in the attack week and in-hospital mortality of patients already admitted rises 34-38%, implying between 42 and 67 Medicare deaths in 2016-2021 Neprash et al. (2026). In a small California sample of 8 attacks, ED visits fell 16.21% in week 2 while visits at nearby unattacked hospitals rose 6.7%-7.1% Abouk and Powell (2024).
  • Event studies find large firm costs: a breach of customers' personal data cuts the average target's market value 1.1% (about $607 million) and sales growth 3.2 percentage points Kamiya et al. (2021); a matched difference-in-differences finds breaches raise total liabilities about 12.9% to fund remediation, while ransomware cuts gross profit and operating income Mutallimov et al. (2026); and bank breaches disrupt deposits and lending Durongkadej and Wang (2025).
  • On fraud, a randomized online experiment in Kenya finds standard scam-detection tips do not improve identification of scam messages and raise false suspicion of legitimate ones Kubilay et al. (2023). Descriptive data show cyber-enabled fraud nearly tripled to around 2.5 million cases in 2022 and remains underreported; industry estimates put scam losses at 2.5%-4.2% of GDP in some developing countries Khiaonarong and Zheng (2026).
  • In Kenya, firm-survey regressions associate a virus attack with about 35% lower labor productivity (46% for large firms) and online crime with 27% lower productivity; upskilling mitigates losses, especially for SMEs, while IT security capabilities raise productivity but do not offset breach losses Tetteh and Otioma (2024). Magnitudes are sensitive to specification and rest on one cross-sectional survey.
  • Evidence on disclosure rules is thin: state breach-notification laws are associated with less identity theft in difference-in-differences estimates, though the effect is imprecise and likely modest Romanosky et al. (2011); 10-K cybersecurity disclosures mandated by the SEC in 2023 vary widely in quality Haapamäki and Sihvonen (2026); firms' qualitative disclosures only partly reflect incident costs Mutallimov et al. (2026); and honeypot data show vulnerability-disclosure timing shapes attack diffusion Mitra and Ransbotham (2015).
  • Country and public-sector costs come from case studies, not causal estimates: Costa Rica's 2022 ransomware crisis cost up to 2.4% of GDP by a secondary estimate, with US$31.5 million in direct recovery costs and 49 services disrupted for 24-204 days, in a study co-produced with the government de Salins et al. (2026); WannaCry cost England's NHS about £92 million Ghafur et al. (2019).
  • On capacity and security investment, evidence is descriptive: 89% of high-income countries have a national incident-response team, against 46% of lower-income countries with an operational one, though the index measures commitments, not outcomes International Telecommunication Union (2024); an early cost synthesis finds defensive spending exceeds direct losses for many traditional crimes moved online Anderson et al. (2013); and cyber insurers rely on coverage caps rather than risk-based pricing Ning (2026).

Mechanisms

  • Ransomware is an availability shock, breaches a balance-sheet shock: ransomware cuts gross profit, operating income and receivables, while breaches expand liabilities to fund remediation Mutallimov et al. (2026); when hospitals are hit, emergency demand shifts to nearby hospitals Abouk and Powell (2024).
  • Lost trust adds costs beyond remediation: breached customers cut engagement in the breached online channel Janakiraman et al. (2018), bank breaches disrupt deposit and loan growth Durongkadej and Wang (2025), and weak board risk oversight enlarges losses Kamiya et al. (2021).
  • Shocks spread through networks: in a Fedwire payment-network simulation, an attack on large banks transmits liquidity stress to healthy banks, with vulnerability up about 50% during the COVID-19 shock Eisenbach et al. (2025); one pipeline attack spilled into energy commodity markets Goodell and Corbet (2023).
  • Generic awareness can backfire: legitimate financial messages share the red flags that scam tips teach, so tips raise false positives and can erode trust in mobile money Kubilay et al. (2023).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Most causal evidence concerns adoption and use, measuring incident costs to firms and hospitals; policy reform is covered only by breach-notification laws Romanosky et al. (2011), programs only by a scam-tips experiment Kubilay et al. (2023), and no causal study evaluates security investment, national incident-response teams or capacity building.
  • Causal estimates come almost entirely from the United States; developing-country evidence is limited to Kenyan studies Kubilay et al. (2023), Tetteh and Otioma (2024) and a Costa Rica case de Salins et al. (2026), and no causal estimate exists of an incident's cost to a national economy.
  • No study covers labor-market or environmental outcomes; public-sector costs rest on case accounting de Salins et al. (2026), Ghafur et al. (2019), and fraud data are underreported and partly industry-sourced Khiaonarong and Zheng (2026), leaving the scale of scam losses in developing countries uncertain.
  • No study estimates returns to security spending or compares defense costs with avoided losses beyond an early accounting synthesis Anderson et al. (2013), and effects of the SEC's 2023 disclosure rule on incidents or firm value are untested Haapamäki and Sihvonen (2026).
