Data governance30 studies · 19 causalQuasi-experimental studies, mostly of the EU's GDPR, consistently find privacy rules impose costs that fall hardest on small firms: EU firms cut data storage 26% relative to US firms Demirer et al. (2024), and web-vendor concentration rose Peukert et al. (2022). Benefits are rarely measured; developing countries lack causal evidence.

What the evidence shows

  • In difference-in-differences estimates, GDPR led EU firms to cut data storage 26% and processing 15% relative to US firms, consistent with a 20% rise in the cost of data, larger for small firms Demirer et al. (2024); EU website page views and e-commerce revenue fell about 12% Goldberg et al. (2024); and data-intensive EU firms' profit margins grew 1.7 to 3.4 percentage points less than US peers' Koski and Valmari (2020).
  • Innovation effects are mixed. In a panel of 4.1 million Google Play apps, GDPR induced the exit of about a third of apps and halved new entry, and a structural model implies consumer surplus fell by about a third Janßen et al. (2022); a German difference-in-differences shows a shift to incremental innovation, with new-to-firm sales shares up 0.9-3.3 percentage points and new-to-market shares down 0.6-1.5 points Blind et al. (2022).
  • Difference-in-differences studies find GDPR reduced deals and capital raised by EU tech ventures relative to US and rest-of-world peers, most for newer, data-related and consumer-facing ventures Jia et al. (2021). Websites cut third-party vendors, even outside the EU, and concentration rose as Google gained share Peukert et al. (2022), Johnson et al. (2023). CCPA's passage moved retailer stocks only for intangible-intensive firms, which earned positive abnormal returns in an event study Patel et al. (2023).
  • Restricting tracking weakens advertising: a difference-in-differences study finds the EU e-Privacy Directive cut display-ad effectiveness by about 65% Goldfarb and Tucker (2011); Apple's App Tracking Transparency reduced ad-supported app monetization, most for smaller developers Kesler (2022); the COPPA settlement cut YouTube kids'-content monetization Johnson et al. (2026); and a structural analysis finds GDPR's opt-in rule shrank the tracked consumer pool 12.5%, though remaining consumers became more valuable to advertisers Aridor et al. (2023).
  • Difference-in-differences studies of the EU Digital Markets Act find early shifts: a browser choice screen raised Firefox usage 91% on iOS and 13% on Android from month 15, though iOS gains went mostly to Chrome, not smaller browsers Akesson et al. (2026); after Google stopped self-preferencing Maps, EU map-related searches and Google Maps traffic rose more than 21% relative to non-EU markets Pape and Rossi (2026).
  • Data-flow evidence is weaker: in a difference-in-differences design, Japanese firms that began transferring data abroad saw 4-5% higher labor productivity and 5-6% higher TFP, though more productive firms self-select Ito and Tomiura (2025); a CGE model estimates localization cuts GDP by 0.1% to 1.7% and domestic investment by up to 4.2% Bauer et al. (2014); and a legal database finds 12 of 121 economies require localizing all personal data Molinuevo et al. (2025).
  • Benefits are less often measured: state breach-notification laws are associated with less identity theft, though the effect is imprecise and likely modest Romanosky et al. (2011); open government data has seeded firms, some with billion-dollar valuations, per case evidence only Zeleti et al. (2016); and GDPR did not materially reduce users' exposure to the main app SDK ecosystems Jin et al. (2024).

Mechanisms

  • Compliance costs weigh more on smaller firms and vendors, shifting share to incumbents: smaller firms faced larger increases in the cost of data Demirer et al. (2024), and Google lost less business than smaller vendors after GDPR Peukert et al. (2022).
  • Data and computation are strong complements, so a higher cost of data also cuts computation and raises the production cost of information, by 4% on average Demirer et al. (2024).
  • Consent rules shrink targeting data, but opt-outs leave a more predictable pool, partly offsetting losses Aridor et al. (2023); ad losses concentrate among general-content publishers and plain display formats that cannot substitute rich content for targeting Goldfarb and Tucker (2011).
  • Distance raises investors' information costs: the GDPR venture pullback is larger for investors farther from the venture Jia et al. (2021), and distant US investors cut funding to EU data-intensive startups more than domestic EU investors Jia et al. (2025).

Where the evidence is thin

  • Nearly all causal evidence evaluates policy and regulatory reform; no study evaluates public investment or programs, such as open-data platforms or data infrastructure, and adoption and use is covered only by Japanese firms starting cross-border data transfers Ito and Tomiura (2025).
  • Causal evidence covers the EU, the US and Japan; developing countries appear only in a legal database Molinuevo et al. (2025), a review World Bank (2021), a CGE model Bauer et al. (2014) and cross-country correlations Ferracane and van der Marel (2024), so effects of their data-protection and localization laws are unmeasured.
  • No causal study covers labor markets, inclusion, the public sector or the environment, and none values consumers' privacy gains, so the welfare balance of privacy rules, which theory leaves ambiguous Acquisti et al. (2016), is unresolved.
  • Horizons are short and costs incomplete: DMA evidence covers the first 15+ months Akesson et al. (2026), some GDPR evidence only 6 months after enforcement Peukert et al. (2022), and no study measures regulators' enforcement costs or the cost-effectiveness of data-protection authorities.

How the evidence is classified

What the study evaluates

Policy-based and investment operations need different evidence. Each study is tagged by what it actually evaluates; a study of a bundle — a platform plus a mandate to use it — carries more than one tag.

Strength of identification

The repository separates studies that can support a causal claim from those that document an association. Both are useful — but only the first two categories below license statements of the form “X caused Y to change by Z”.

Sources and method. Entries are drawn from peer-reviewed economics journals, NBER and CEPR working papers, World Bank Policy Research Working Papers, and publications of the IMF, OECD, ILO, ITU and allied agencies, together with working papers circulated on SSRN and arXiv. The grading reflects the identification strategy the authors themselves use.

Caveats. A strong design does not make an estimate universally valid: most entries identify a local effect for one population, one technology generation and one period. Magnitudes are reported as stated in the source. Where a study reports many estimates, the entry gives the headline result. Follow the link on each entry back to the paper before citing a number.
